title: Performance Enhancing Proxies Intended to Mitigate Link-Related Degradations
summary: Surveys Performance Enhancing Proxies, devices that improve TCP performance on links with troublesome characteristics, such as satellite, wireless WAN, and wireless LAN. It discusses the tradeoffs of using them.

eli5.summary: Some roads are bumpy and slow, so helpers along the way make the trip smoother for the cars.

questions: what is a performance enhancing proxy
how does snoop improve tcp over wireless
subtitle: A survey of the middleboxes that speed up TCP over satellite and wireless links, and what they cost.

tldr.problem: TCP performs badly on links with long delays, high error rates, outages or very lopsided bandwidth, such as satellite and wireless links.
tldr.mechanism: Performance Enhancing Proxies (PEPs) sit on the path and tweak TCP or the application protocol, for example by acknowledging data locally, retransmitting locally, compressing headers or splitting the connection in two.
tldr.outcome: The RFC makes no recommendation for or against PEPs. It warns that they can break end-to-end semantics and rule out end-to-end IPsec, so they should be used only where end-to-end fixes are not available and the user stays in control.

today: RFC 3135 is an Informational survey from June 2001, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It does not standardize anything; it describes PEP techniques as they stood then and the trade-offs of using them.

sections.title: What a PEP Is and Why It Exists
sections.content:
TCP is used by many Internet and intranet applications, but on some links its performance is limited by the link's own characteristics. A Performance Enhancing Proxy (PEP) is used to improve the performance of Internet protocols on network paths where native performance suffers because of a link or subnetwork on the path.

The document is a survey. It is informational and makes no recommendation for or against PEPs. It does say that the authors believe the end-to-end principle should stay the prevailing approach, and that PEPs should be used only in specific environments where end-to-end mechanisms with similar benefits are not available. Where a PEP is used, the end user (or sometimes the network administrator) should know about it and control whether it is used, so the user can always choose plain end-to-end IP.

Standards track recommendations for individual link problems, such as high error rates, low bandwidth or asymmetric bandwidth, come from the Performance Implications of Link Characteristics (PILC) working group. The RFC also says new link technologies should be designed so these techniques are not required, if at all possible.
sections.eli5: A PEP is a helper in the middle of the road that makes a slow or bumpy stretch easier for traffic. The authors say it is best used only when nothing simpler works, and you should be able to say no to it.

sections.title: Ways PEPs Differ
sections.content:
The RFC sorts PEPs along several axes.

  • Layering: transport layer PEPs (most of them work with TCP, and are called TCP PEPs) leave the application protocol alone. Application layer PEPs, such as web caches and relay mail transfer agents with link-specific tuning, can also trim extra round trips and verbose headers.
  • Distribution: an integrated PEP is one component in one node. A distributed PEP has two or more components, typically one at each end of the problem link, such as a satellite hop.
  • Symmetry: a symmetric PEP acts the same in both directions. An asymmetric PEP acts differently per direction, which suits links whose two directions differ.
  • Split connections: the PEP ends the TCP connection from one host and opens a separate one toward the other. This allows, for example, window scaling over a long link when one end system cannot use it. It also means the PEP acknowledges data on its own.
  • Transparency: a PEP may need no change to the end systems, or may need changes at one or both ends. Transparency is not the same as preserving end-to-end semantics: ACK spacing keeps them, while a split connection may not.
sections.eli5: Helpers come in different kinds. Some work on the whole trip, some on just one stretch. Some work quietly, and some need the drivers to know about them.

sections.title: PEP Mechanisms
sections.content:
A PEP may combine several mechanisms. The main ones in the RFC are:

  • ACK spacing: smooths out bunched acknowledgments so the sender does not send bursts of data.
  • Local acknowledgments: the PEP acknowledges data itself, which speeds up slow start on paths with a large bandwidth*delay product. The PEP then has to recover any data dropped after it acknowledged it.
  • Local retransmissions: the PEP resends data lost between itself and the receiver. Snoop caches segments, watches for duplicate ACKs, resends from its cache and hides the duplicate ACKs from the sender.
  • ACK filtering and reconstruction: on highly asymmetric paths, ACKs are filtered on one side of the link and rebuilt on the other.
  • Tunneling: messages are encapsulated to cross a link, or to force traffic through the PEP endpoints.
  • Compression: TCP and IP header compression (for example RFC 1144) and payload compression. Payload compression must happen before encryption, because encrypted data no longer compresses.
  • Handling disconnection: a PEP can keep the last ACK and send it with a window of zero so the sender goes into persist mode, or in a split connection can hide the outage from the far host.
  • Priority-based multiplexing: interactive traffic gets the slow link ahead of background transfers.
  • Protocol boosters: for example adding the optional UDP checksum, parity packets for forward error correction, or timestamps for jitter control.
sections.eli5: Helpers have many tricks: giving quick thumbs-up so the sender keeps going, resending lost items from a nearby copy, shrinking the packages, and letting urgent mail go first.

sections.title: Costs: The End-to-End Argument
sections.content:
Most of the downsides of PEPs come from the chance of breaking the end-to-end semantics of a connection, which is a main reason the RFC does not recommend them for general use. Not every PEP breaks them, and a correctly designed one only adds optimizations to a subpath.

  • Fate sharing: if connection state lives in a PEP and the PEP crashes, the connection dies even when another path exists. Users may accept that risk, but it should be their choice.
  • End-to-end reliability: a TCP ACK only shows data reached the other TCP, not the application. A PEP that acknowledges application data too early removes the end-to-end guarantee. The RFC notes that application layer PEPs for relayed email can be fine if they behave like a regular relay MTA.
  • Failure diagnostics: a PEP can delay failure detection, and tools such as PING and traceroute may give misleading results because they can bypass or be answered by the PEP.
  • Asymmetric routing: traffic usually has to pass through the PEP in both directions, although ACK spacing needs only the ACK direction.
  • Mobile hosts: PEP state may need to move during handoff.
  • Scalability: PEPs need more processing and per-connection memory than routers, so they will always be a step behind routers in throughput.
sections.eli5: A helper in the middle can hide problems, lose track of your trip if it breaks, and say a package arrived when it has not reached you yet. That is why you should know it is there.

sections.title: PEPs and IPsec
sections.content:
Security is the heaviest cost. The RFC says that breaking end-to-end semantics disables end-to-end use of IPsec: with ESP encryption the TCP header and payload are unreadable to the PEP, so it may not work well or at all. In general, a user or administrator must choose between PEPs and IPsec.

Workarounds exist but add complexity: using IPsec only for some traffic, running IPsec between the two PEPs of a distributed PEP, or making the PEP an IPsec endpoint. All of them leave traffic exposed inside the PEP, and the end systems may wrongly assume the stronger security level they negotiated covers the whole path. The RFC also notes that a PEP is a good place from which to launch denial of service or man in the middle attacks, so it must be protected like any other network device.
sections.eli5: A sealed envelope cannot be helped along if the helper cannot read the address. To help, the helper must open it, and then you have to trust the helper.

sections.title: Satellite, Wireless WAN and Wireless LAN
sections.content:
The RFC illustrates PEPs in three environments.

VSAT (satellite) networks use geosynchronous satellites in a star topology. Propagation delay runs from 240 to 280 milliseconds one way, so round trip time is at least 480 milliseconds from propagation alone. The outroute is usually far larger than the inroute, with ratios of 400 to 1 or more becoming common. VSAT PEPs usually use an asymmetric distributed split connection with local acknowledgments and retransmissions, plus compression.

Wireless WAN links (GSM, GPRS, CDPD and others) can have bandwidth as low as a few hundred bits per second, round trips near one second, long outages and expensive use. The RFC describes the Mowgli system and the Wireless Application Protocol (WAP), in which a WAP proxy translates between the mobile terminal and ordinary web servers.

Wireless LANs offer 1 Mbps to 11 Mbps and round trips of a few to tens of milliseconds, but suffer bit errors, collisions and handoff losses that TCP misreads as congestion. Snoop, a TCP-aware agent in the base station, retransmits locally and suppresses duplicate ACKs. It needs to see the unencrypted traffic and both data and ACKs through the same base station.
sections.eli5: Satellite trips take a long time, phone-network trips are slow and costly, and wifi trips lose packets from bumps. Each kind gets a different kind of helper.
